pizlonator · Oct 17, 2026

I confirmed, it's faster than the Go version, which is very surprising, and super impressive!

Caveats:

- I don't think it's right to say that it's "written in TypeScript". In fact, it's written in the subscript of TypeScript that scriptc supports. scriptc isn't just a subset of ts; it even diverges from ts semantics in sneaky ways to facilitate its optimizations. So, these folks have really created a TypeScript-like native language with some kind of RC-GC hybrid and a bunch of caveats. Not clear if this is any better than just creating a new language.

- Very likely that it was codeveloped with scriptc, so it's getting maximum benefit from exactly the sorts of idioms that scriptc supports well. And, I would bet they landed optimizations to scriptc specifically to get this result.

This could be useful, assuming they invest in supporting it, and you're the sort of person who needs 2x faster ts compiles.

ameliaquining · Oct 17, 2026

Well, if you write a library in the scriptc subset, it will also work in regular JavaScript runtimes, for free. (Unless you rely on, e.g., catching runtime errors thrown by failed casts, but that's easy enough to avoid.) That seems like a clear advantage over creating a new language.

What I do think would be nice would be if all the tweak-JS-semantics-for-optimization-purposes projects (scriptc, Static Hermes, Nova, possibly Closure Compiler) got together and agreed on a minimal set of rules that TypeScript code should follow in order to be compatible with all of them. Then there could be a push for commonly used npm packages to adhere to those rules, and advertise that they do so in order to be fully optimized.
